PF3-F-01.hint: The output of an inverse trig function is an angle. Ask which angle, inside the restricted interval for that function, has the given sine, cosine, or tangent. \(\arcsin\) returns an angle in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), \(\arccos\) in \([0, \pi]\), and \(\arctan\) in \(\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
slips: Giving an angle outside the restricted interval, such as \(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\) for \(\arccos\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) instead of \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).
Reading \(\arcsin x\) as \(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\). The \(-1\) in \(\sin^{-1}\) means inverse function, not reciprocal.
Giving \(\dfrac{11\pi}{6}\) for \(\arcsin\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\) instead of \(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\). The output must lie in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

PF3-F-02.hint: The input to \(\arcsin\) or \(\arccos\) is a sine or cosine value, so the domain is \([-1, 1]\). The input to \(\arctan\) can be any real number. The range is the restricted interval of the original function. Shifts and stretches change the domain or range in the usual way.
slips: Swapping the domain and range of an inverse trig function.
Giving the range of \(\arccos\) as \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\). That interval belongs to \(\arcsin\).
Giving all real numbers as the domain of \(\arcsin\) or \(\arccos\).

PF3-A-01.hint: For an expression like \(\tan(\arccos x)\), let the inside be an angle \(\theta\), draw a right triangle that fits it, find the missing side, and read off the ratio. For \(\arccos(\cos\theta)\), check whether \(\theta\) is already in \([0, \pi]\). If it is not, find the angle in \([0, \pi]\) with the same cosine.
slips: Canceling \(\arccos(\cos\theta)\) to \(\theta\) without checking that \(\theta\) is in \([0, \pi]\).
Choosing a negative missing side when the angle from \(\arccos\) must be in \([0, \pi]\), where the sine is never negative.
Mixing up the adjacent and opposite sides when reading the ratio from the triangle.

Let \(\theta = \arcsin\left(-\dfrac{7}{25}\right)\). The angle from \(\arcsin\) is in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), where the cosine is never negative. Draw a right triangle with the known side \(7\) and hypotenuse \(25\): the other side is \(24\), so the cosine is \(\dfrac{24}{25}\). Then \(\cos\theta = \dfrac{24}{25}\).

The inverse function returns an angle in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\), and \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\) is not in that interval, so the answer is not \(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\). Find the angle in \(\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\) with the same sine: it is \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\).
